Advanced reactivity
in Owl

RD Framework JS - Géry Debongnie

Owl 3

Signals and computations

A primer on Owl 3

A quick overview.

Ground rules

An Owl 3 component

Two signals, a value derived from them, something that happens when it changes, and a template bound to all of it.

order_line.js

class OrderLine extends Component {
    static template = "sale.OrderLine";

    qty = signal(1);
    price = signal(9.99);

    total = computed(() => this.qty() * this.price());

    setup() {
        useEffect(() => {
            document.title = `Total: ${this.total()}`;
        });
    }

    add() {
        this.qty.set(this.qty() + 1);
    }
}

order_line.xml

<t t-name="sale.OrderLine">
    <input t-model="this.qty"/>
    <button t-on-click="this.add">+1</button>
    <p>Total: <t t-out="this.total()"/></p>
</t>
  • Nothing declaresNo dependency list ties total to qty, and none ties the effect to total.

Type in the box and total recomputes and the title changes. Nobody wired that up, and how it happens is the rest of the talk.

Ground rules

Three primitives

Everything in this talk is one of these, or the graph they make between them.

const count = signal(0);

count();        // read
count.set(1);   // write

const double = computed(() => count() * 2);

useEffect(() => {
    document.title = `count: ${double()}`;
});
  • signalA value you own. Call it to read, set it to write.
  • computedA value derived from other values. It caches itself, and never runs if nothing reads it.
  • useEffectA change to something outside the graph. It re-runs when what it read changes.

All three read the same way, and that read is what the rest of this talk is about.

Derived values

computed values

Owl 2 — three moving parts

setup() {
    this.state = useState({ total: 0 });

    onWillRender(() => {
        const key = this.props.orders.length;
        if (key !== this._key) {
            this._key = key;
            const total = expensive(this.props.orders);
            this.state.total = total;
        }
    });
}

Owl 3 — one

total = computed(() =>
    expensive(this.props.orders)
);
  • CachedIt does not recompute unless something it read changed.
  • DeclaredThe dependency is now written down. The runtime can see it.

The trigger moved: Owl 2 recomputed because a component was about to render, Owl 3 because the state it read changed.

The shift

A change of paradigm

The centre of the framework moves. Rendering stops being the thing everything is arranged around, and state takes its place.

The component tree has not gone anywhere. But the important part is the state relationships

Signals

Bridging the gap

  • t-ref fills a signal: signal.ref() holds the element, and null until the component is mounted. No separate useRef.
  • t-model binds a signal to an input, both ways.

todo_list.js

import { signal, computed, useEffect } from "@odoo/owl";

export class TodoList extends Component {
    input = signal.ref();
    name = signal("");

    greeting = computed(() => `Hello ${this.name()}`);

    setup() {
        useEffect(() => this.input()?.focus());
    }
}

todo_list.xml

<input t-ref="this.input"
       placeholder="What needs doing?"/>

<input t-model="this.name"/>
<p t-out="this.greeting()"/>

One concept fewer to hold: refs, model bindings and state are all the same thing - so a computed reads what t-model writes, with nothing in between.

The state and the DOM, in one graph: what the user types is a signal, and so is the element they type it in.

Reactivity

What is it for?

The question

Change a value. Something updates.

const price = signal(100);
const qty   = signal(2);

const total = computed(() => price() * qty());

effect(() => {
    console.log("total is", total());
});
// logs: total is 200

qty.set(4);
await nextTick();
// logs: total is 400

qty.set(2);     // divided by 2
price.set(200); // multiplied by 2
await nextTick();
// no logs
  • Nobodytold total that qty had changed.
  • Nobodytold the effect that total had changed.
  • Nobodywrote down that any of the three were connected at all.

And yet exactly one log line came out, with the right number in it.

SoHow did it know? That is the whole talk.

Ground rules

A signal, on its own

  • If you were at the Owl 3 talk this is a minute of revision. If not, this is everything you need.
import { signal } from "@odoo/owl";

const price = signal(100);

price();          // 100   - call it to read
price.set(120);   //       - set it to write
price();          // 120
  • A valueHeld in a cell. That is all a signal is.
  • Two operationsCall to read, set to write. There is no third.
  • The read mattersCalling it is not just fetching. It is how the runtime learns you care.

One value, two operations, and that is the entire primitive.

Two models

Owl 2 vs Owl 3

  • Both track your reads. They differ on who the read subscribes, and when that was decided.

Owl 2 — the proxy carries its watcher

// useState is reactive(obj, cb), and cb is
// "re-render this component"
const state = useState({ n: 0 });

state.n;   // subscribes the component this proxy
           // was made for. Only ever that one.

One proxy, one watcher, fixed at the moment it was created. Hold a different proxy over the same object and you wake a different component.

Owl 3 — a signal is just a signal

const n = signal(0);

n();       // wakes whatever computation is
           // running right now. Decided here,
           // at the read.

The signal carries nothing. The context you read it in is the observer — a render, a computed, an effect.

Which is the granularity too: Owl 2, a component subscribes and re-renders. Owl 3, a computation subscribes and re-runs.

Ground rules

Every shape is signals underneath

You pick a shape to suit the data. The graph only ever sees signals, one per key.

four ways to write the same node

const state = signal.Object({ n: 0 });
state.n;               // a read of one signal

const items = signal.Array([]);
items[0];              // a read of one signal

const conf = proxy({ ui: { dense: true } });
conf.ui.dense;         // a read, one level down

props = useProps();     // a class field
this.props.someNumber;  // props, too
  • One per keyA signal.Object is a signal for each key, not one signal for the object. Read n and you are subscribed to n alone.
  • Same for itemssignal.Array does it per item, and proxy does it level by level as you read deeper.
  • Props as wellThe object useProps hands you is signal-backed, so this.props.someNumber is a tracked read.

The shapes are ergonomics. The gate, the batching and untrack land the same way on all of them.

The shift

You used to design a component tree.
Now you design a computation graph.

  • Owl 2

    Decompose the UI and pass props down. A derived value is a field you keep in sync by hand, on every hook that might change it.

    setup() {
  this.double = this.props.count * 2;
  onWillUpdateProps((next) => {
    this.double = next.count * 2;
  });
}

  • Owl 3

    Start from state, and declare the computations that follow from it: derived values, effects, the render itself. The edge from count to double is built by reading it.

    props = useProps();

double = computed(() => this.props.count * 2);

The shift

Where it comes from does not matter

  • Owl 2

    A reactive value has to be attached to the component that reads it, with useState. Read it without, and nothing re-renders.

    setup() {
  const someService = useService("some_service");
  this.state = useState(
    someService.someReactiveValue()
  );
}

  • Owl 3

    A signal needs no attaching. From a plugin, a prop or a module, reading it is what subscribes whatever is running.

    somePlugin = usePlugin(SomePlugin);

// and then read
this.somePlugin.someSignal();

The Computation Graph

Three kinds of node, and one rule for building edges.

Reactivity

Computations

Can manage dependencies. Three kinds, and one mechanism under all of them: each reads signals, and re-runs when what it read changes.

  • 1

    Rendering a component

    Reads signals, writes DOM. This is the one you already have.

    <t t-out="this.someValue()"/>
  • 2

    A computed value

    Reads signals, returns a value, and holds on to it until one of them changes.

    a = signal(3);
b = signal(5);
sum = computed(() =>
    this.a() + this.b()
);
  • 3

    An effect

    Reads signals, and changes something outside the graph: the document, storage, a library that knows nothing about this one.

    useEffect(() => {
    console.log(this.a(), this.b());
});

A render is not a special case. It is a computation that happens to paint.

Ground rules

Signals (and computations) can be watched

signal — holds a value

const price = signal(100);

price();   // not a subscription
           // just a read
<!-- this is a subscription! -->
<t t-out="this.price()"/>

an effect — changes the world

effect(() => {
    // this is a subscription!
    console.log(price());
});
// runs now, and again whenever
// what it read changes

price.set(120) → the effect logs, the template re-renders. And nothing else in the program ran.

The graph

That example, as a graph

Two signals, one computed, one effect — and a render, which is a computation like any other.

Implicit dependencies

The graph is discovered, never declared.

The edges are implicit: you never write them. There is no dependency array to keep in sync, and no way for it to disagree with the code — because the reads are the declaration.

The graph is dynamic: every time a computation re-runs, it starts from scratch, so it is always correct.

The graph

A write pushes. A read pulls.

A write is cheap and shallow. The work happens when somebody actually wants the answer.

The graph

The Diamond Problem

The diamond: a feeds b and c, d reads both — and an effect reads d, or nothing would ever pull it.

The design being avoided: recompute on write

a.set(2);
//  -> b recomputes        b = 4
//  -> d recomputes now    d = "4/10"   ← a pair
//  -> c recomputes        c = 20      that never existed
//  -> d recomputes again  d = "4/20"

Two runs of d for one write, and between them a value nobody ever set. That is a glitch.

What Owl does: mark, then pull

a.set(2);
//  b, c       stale     (read a directly)
//  d          pending   (check my sources)
//  the effect queued    (flush on the microtask)
//  ...and nothing has been computed at all
// then the flush pulls, and the pull computes:
//  b = 4, c = 20, d = "4/20"   ← once, correct

The write only marks, and marking twice is free. A computed runs when something reads it; effects and renders read on the next microtask.

Step by step

executed / stale / pending / queued

Whatever read a directly is stale — it must re-run. Everything further down is pending — something moved upstream, go ask your sources. The effect is not a value, so it joins a queue instead.

Four flags and one queue push, and a.set(2) returns. Not one compute function has run.

Step by step

Flushing in a microtask

On the microtask the queue drains. The effect asks for d, d asks its sources, and the values come back up the way the question went down.

Four computations, in that order, each one run once — and d never sees a b and a c that disagree.

Fast,
by doing nothing

The two behaviours that make the graph cheap.

The gate

Propagation stops at an unchanged value

The check is on what the computed returns — not on whether its inputs moved.

gate.mjs

const n = signal(1);
const isPositive = computed(() => n() > 0);

effect(() => { isPositive(); downstream++; });

n.set(2);  await tick();
n.set(3);  await tick();
// n moved twice. how often did the effect run?

n.set(-1); await tick();

the graph

Object.is by default. Pass equals: false to notify on every write, for a value you mutate in place.

Laziness

A computed nobody reads never runs

Not "runs and throws the answer away". Does not run.

lazy.mjs

const s = signal(0);
const lazy = computed(() => { runs++; return s() * 2; });

s.set(1);
s.set(2);
s.set(3);
await tick();
// runs so far?

lazy();   // 6

output

recomputes before first read: 0
value: 6 | recomputes after read: 1
  • WhyA write marks observers stale. Marking is not computing.
  • SoA screen you are not looking at costs nothing, even while its data churns.

An effect is the exception: it has no value to pull, so it runs on its own. Effects are the roots that drive everything.

Laziness

Reads outside a computation are free

A read subscribes whatever computation is running. In an event handler, none is.

counter.js

class Counter extends Component {
    static template = "my_module.Counter";

    value = signal(0);

    onClick() {
        // no computation running here:
        // reads the value, subscribes nothing
        console.log(this.value());
    }
}

The gate

Which is why memoisation is free

Laziness and the gate together are the caching you used to write by hand — and this time it composes.

What you used to write

onWillRender(() => {
    const key = this.props.orders.length;
    if (key !== this._key) {
        this._key = key;
        this._total = expensive(this.props.orders);
    }
    this.state.total = this._total;
});

You had to know what to invalidate. And another addon patching expensive made the key silently wrong.

What replaces it

total = computed(() => expensive(this.props.orders));
  • No keyThe reads are the key, and they are recorded on every run.
  • ComposesA computed over a computed inherits both the laziness and the gate.

Nobody writes a cache key, so nobody gets the cache key wrong.

The gate

Comparisons

  • Object.is on a fresh array is always false: a filter recomputes to a new array every time, so the gate never holds.

The problem

visible = computed(() =>
    this.todos.filter((t) => t.text.includes(q))
);
// same contents, new array object
// -> every downstream render re-runs

The fix

import { shallowEqual } from "@odoo/owl";

visible = computed(
    () => this.todos.filter(/* ... */),
    { equals: shallowEqual },
);

Now the gate compares contents, and an unchanged filter result stops the propagation dead.

The rule of thumb: a computed that returns a fresh object or array every time wants an equals.

Miscellaneous

Scheduling

When each computation runs

  • TypeEager / lazyScheduling
  • Template renderingeageron the next microtask, applied on the next animation frame
  • computed valueslazyno scheduling: computed when read
  • Effectseagerimmediately, then on each microtask

Effects

Batched, and cleaned up

three writes in a row

const s = signal(0);
effect(() => log.push(s()));

s.set(1); s.set(2); s.set(3);
await tick();
effect saw: [ 0, 3 ]

Once immediately, then once for the batch — landing on the final value. The intermediates never existed as far as the effect is concerned.

returning a cleanup

effect(() => {
    const v = t();
    trace.push(`run ${v}`);
    return () => trace.push(`cleanup ${v}`);
});
run 0 | cleanup 0 | run 1 |
cleanup 1 | run 2 | cleanup 2

Before every re-run, and once more on dispose. This is where a listener or a timer goes.

Whatever you start in an effect, stop it in the function that effect returns.

Effects

effect and useEffect

useEffect is effect, called in a component or a plugin — and cleaned up for you when that is destroyed.

effect — you dispose it

const stop = effect(() => {
    console.log(value());
});

// later, by hand
stop();

useEffect — disposed with its owner

class Clock extends Component {
    setup() {
        useEffect(() => {
            console.log(this.value());
        });
    }
}
// Clock destroyed: the effect goes too

In a plugin's setup as well: there it lives as long as the plugins around it, and goes when they do.

Effects

Sub-effects

  • Any effect() called while another effect is on the stack becomes its child — even from inside a helper three calls down.
  • When the parent re-runs, its previous children are disposed first.
effect(() => {          // parent
    console.log("parent");

    effect(() => {      // child, owned by it
        console.log(someSignal());
        return () => console.log("child cleanup");
    });
});
  • ImplicitNothing in the child says who owns it. The call stack decided.
  • Each re-runThe old child is disposed, a fresh one created. Cleanup fires every time.
  • Usually rightIt is what you want when the inner effect really is per-run. It is a trap when it is not.

Which is fine — until someone creates the inner one conditionally.

Effects

untrack: read without subscribing

  • It breaks tracking — and it breaks ownership.

Reading without an edge

const c = computed(() => {
    const tracked = s();
    const free = untrack(() => s());
    return tracked + free;
});
// c depends on s once, not twice

And escaping ownership

disposeInner = untrack(() =>
    effect(() => { inner(); })
);

output, the same test as before

inner effect saw: [ 0, 9 ]
survived the parent's re-run
  • Your job nowAn effect created inside untrack has no owner. You dispose it, or it leaks.

Reach for it deliberately and rarely. Most code that wants untrack actually wants the next slide.

A common trap

No cycle allowed

A computed reads its sources to compute. If two of them read each other, the reading never bottoms out.

cart.js

class Cart extends Component {
    static template = "my_module.Cart";

    price = signal(100);

    total = computed(() => this.price() + this.tax());
    tax = computed(() => this.total() * 0.2);
}

reading this.total()

RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded

total reads tax, which reads total, which reads tax… Nothing catches it earlier: the stack does. The graph has to point one way — derive both from the same source instead.

Practical Tips

A common trap

Keep the signal, read it late

  • Don't do this

    The signal is read once, in setup. The template gets a plain value, and never hears of a change.

    somePlugin = usePlugin(SomePlugin);
someValue = this.somePlugin.someSignal();
    <t t-out="this.someValue"/>

  • Do this

    Keep the signal itself, and read it in the template: the render subscribes, and re-runs when it changes.

    somePlugin = usePlugin(SomePlugin);
someSignal = this.somePlugin.someSignal;
    <t t-out="this.someSignal()"/>

A common trap

Give the signal, not the value

  • Give the value

    The parent reads the signal as it renders, so the parent subscribes. Every change re-renders the parent, to hand the child a new number.

    <!-- parent -->
<SomeChild value="this.value()"/>

<!-- child -->
<t t-out="this.props.value"/>

  • Give the signal

    The parent passes the signal itself and reads nothing. Only the child, which reads it, subscribes — and only the child re-renders.

    <!-- parent -->
<SomeChild value="this.value"/>

<!-- child -->
<t t-out="this.props.value()"/>

Design

Derive, don't store.

Anything you can compute from something else should be a computed, not a second piece of state you keep in sync.

  • Store, and keep in sync

    Two signals that must agree, and an effect to make them. Until it runs, they do not.

    count = signal(1);
double = signal(2);

setup() {
    useEffect(() => {
        this.double.set(this.count() * 2);
    });
}

  • Derive

    One signal, and a computed that cannot disagree with it.

    count = signal(1);
double = computed(() => this.count() * 2);

Two facts that must agree are a bug waiting for a deadline.

Design

Make everything reactive

A computed only knows about what it reads through a signal. A plain field slips past it.

  • Mixing raw values and signals

    this.value is read, but not tracked: change it, and total keeps the old answer until counter happens to move.

    value = 10;
counter = signal(1);

total = computed(() =>
    this.value + this.counter()
);

  • Signals all the way

    Both reads are tracked, so a change to either one recomputes total.

    value = signal(10);
counter = signal(1);

total = computed(() =>
    this.value() + this.counter()
);

Design

Make a readonly version

Hand out a computed that reads the signal: the same value, just as reactive, and nothing to write to.

some_plugin.js

mySignal = signal(1);
myReadonlySignal = computed(() => this.mySignal());

this.myReadonlySignal();      // 1, and it tracks
this.myReadonlySignal.set(2); // throws: read-only
this.mySignal.set(2);         // only the owner writes

Design

Do not wrap everything in a proxy

  • Don't do this

    Every field of the model, at every depth, becomes reactive — including the ones that never needed to be. What is state is decided by a wrapper, far from the class.

    this.model = proxy(new Model());

  • Do this

    The class says which of its fields are state. Everything else stays a plain field.

    class Model {
    someState = signal(1);

    someFunction() { ... }
}

this.model = new Model();

Design

Short-circuit with computed

A computed in front of a render is a gate: the render only hears about the result, not about every input that fed it.

  • Read in the template

    The render reads a and b itself, so it subscribes to both. Any change to either re-renders, even when the condition comes out the same.

    <div t-if="this.a() && this.b()">
    ...
</div>

  • Read through a computed

    The render subscribes to isVisible alone. a and b can move all they like: unless the result flips, nothing re-renders.

    isVisible = computed(() => this.a() && this.b());
    <div t-if="this.isVisible()">
    ...
</div>

The tool

useOnChange for explicit dependency tracking

Sometimes you genuinely must write state when something changes — load a record when the id moves. The hook splits in two, so the cycle cannot form.

record_viewer.js

setup() {
    useOnChange(
        // tracked: this half only
        () => [this.props.recordId],

        // not tracked: read and write freely
        async (recordId) => {
            this.record.set(null);
            this.record.set(await load(recordId));
        },
    );
}

The tool

And the dependencies compare by value

Which makes it fire on the change you meant, not on every write upstream of it.

useOnChange(
    () => [this.count() > 10],
    (isBig) => console.log("isBig", isBig),
);

// count 2 -> 3 -> 4 ... nothing.
// the dependency is still false.

// count 10 -> 11: fires once

the plain effect, for contrast

useEffect(() => {
    console.log("isBig", this.count() > 10);
});
// re-runs on every single change of count
  • Use itWhen the callback must read reactive values that should not trigger it, or when the trigger is a derived condition.
  • OtherwiseA plain useEffect is simpler. Do not reach for this by default.

Same gate as a computed, applied to the trigger instead of to the value.

Conclusion

Ground rules

The whole set

Three primitives, and the five names around them. Nothing else to learn.

values

  • signalA value. Call it to read, set it to write.
  • signal.ArrayA list, one signal per item. Shallow.
  • signal.ObjectA bag of keys, one signal per key. Shallow.
  • proxyThe same, every level down, as you read deeper.
  • computedDerived from other values. Cached, and lazy.
  • asyncComputedThe same, for a value that has to be awaited.

reactions

  • effectRuns when what it read changes. Nothing pulls it, so it is what drives the graph at all.
  • useEffectThe same thing inside a component, disposed with it.
  • useOnChangeRun a callback when the values you name change, compared by value.
  • untrackRead without subscribing to what you read.

The last two are the escape hatches — and you have now seen, twice each, why you would want one.

Appendix

Held in reserve, for the questions that come.

Two models

Reactivity

They all render well. Two questions separate them, and each row below moves exactly one.

  • FrameworkWho writes the dependency downYou read a value. Who gets subscribed?So what can observe
  • ReactYou do, by handNobody. The read is not the subscription, owning the state is: a setter re-renders the component either way.A component, when you say so
  • Owl 2The framework, on readWhoever the proxy was made for. useState chose that once; reads only narrow which keys wake it.A component render, nothing else
  • Owl 3The framework, on readWhatever computation is running.Any computation. A render is one of them

Vue 3 and Solid capture the way Owl 3 does: the observer is whatever is running, so a computed can be one.

Two models

Two questions, four answers

Three of them are frameworks. The fourth is what you write when the framework has no answer.

Nobody ships the top left. It is where you end up when the only observer on offer is a component.

Evidence

The diamond, actually run

  • Owl 3 at 3.0.0-alpha.48, counting every recompute.

diamond.mjs

const a = signal(1);
const b = computed(() => { bRuns++; return a() * 2; });
const c = computed(() => { cRuns++; return a() * 10; });
const d = computed(() => { dRuns++; return `${b()}/${c()}`; });

effect(() => seen.push(d()));

a.set(2);   await tick();
a.set(3);   await tick();

output

effect saw: [ '2/10', '4/20', '6/30' ]
recomputes  b: 3   c: 3   d: 3
  • No glitchNo inconsistent pair, ever. 4/10 never appears.
  • No wasteThree changes, three recomputes each. Not four, not six.

Correct and minimal. Those usually trade off; here they fall out of the same design.
